blocks.text: Common OSCE scenarios include:
A 32-year-old woman with heavy menstrual bleeding requests an LNG-IUS.
A woman wants long-term contraception and would prefer lighter periods.
A patient with dysmenorrhoea asks whether an LNG-IUS could help.
A woman with irregular bleeding after insertion requests advice.
A patient with missing IUS threads presents for assessment.
A woman with fibroids asks whether an LNG-IUS is suitable.
A patient with current breast cancer requests hormonal contraception.
A woman wants to conceive and requests removal.
An examiner asks you to counsel a patient about insertion, adverse effects and complications.
A patient with an LNG-IUS in situ develops pelvic pain or a positive pregnancy test.

“Good morning. My name is Dr ____. I understand you are considering a hormonal intrauterine system. I would like to ask about your menstrual cycle, pregnancy plans, medical history and any symptoms you are experiencing. I will explain how the system works, its benefits and possible side effects, and what insertion and removal involve. You can ask questions at any time, and the decision will be yours. Is that alright?”
Before insertion or removal:
Confirm the patient's identity and the intended procedure.
Explain benefits, alternatives, risks and possible discomfort.
Obtain informed consent.
Assess pregnancy risk and medical eligibility.
Discuss pain relief and the expected bleeding pattern.
Explain that the patient can request removal at any time.
Maintain privacy and provide a chaperone for the intimate examination or procedure according to patient preference and local practice.
Use the mnemonic HORMONE.

content_groups.group_title: H — Heavy menstrual bleeding and menstrual history

blocks.text: Ask about:
Date of the last menstrual period.
Regularity, duration and volume of bleeding.
Flooding, clots and frequent changes of sanitary products.
Dysmenorrhoea and pelvic pain.
Symptoms of anaemia, such as fatigue, dizziness and breathlessness.
Intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding.
If the patient has heavy menstrual bleeding, assess whether further investigation is required before attributing it to a benign menstrual disorder.

Current contraceptive use.
Possibility of pregnancy.
Ask about:

Previous pelvic inflammatory disease.
Current STI symptoms.

Unexplained vaginal bleeding.
Ask about:
Current contraception.
Previous hormonal treatments for heavy menstrual bleeding.
Anticoagulants and other medicines that may contribute to bleeding.
Previous LNG-IUS use and adverse effects.
Previous difficult insertion or expulsion.

content_groups.group_title: O — Other symptoms and examination indications

blocks.text: Ask about pelvic pain, fever, abnormal discharge, pressure symptoms or a palpable pelvic mass.
Explore whether she wants:
Contraception alone.
Treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding.
Relief from dysmenorrhoea.
Reduced or absent menstruation.
A reversible method that requires little daily attention.
Check pregnancy risk, medical eligibility and whether the patient understands that irregular bleeding or spotting is common during the first few months.
A pelvic examination is required before insertion. Additional investigations depend on the patient's symptoms and clinical history.
Example: Mirena.
Contains 52 mg levonorgestrel at insertion.
Used for contraception and, where licensed, heavy menstrual bleeding.
May be used for up to eight years for contraception in some jurisdictions; duration for other indications may differ.
Example: Kyleena.
Contains 19.5 mg levonorgestrel.
Primarily indicated for contraception.
Commonly licensed for up to five years.
Example: Jaydess.

Primarily indicated for contraception.
Commonly licensed for up to three years.
Exam point: do not assume all LNG-IUS products have the same dose, licensed duration or indications. Always check the specific device and current local product guidance.
The LNG-IUS releases levonorgestrel locally within the uterine cavity.
Its main actions are:
Thickening of cervical mucus: reduces sperm penetration through the cervix.
Endometrial suppression: causes the endometrium to become thin, reducing menstrual blood loss.
Impaired sperm function: the local progestogen environment reduces sperm survival and function.
Ovulation often continues, particularly with lower-dose systems, although some ovarian suppression can occur.
The LNG-IUS is not an abortifacient and does not terminate an established pregnancy.
The LNG-IUS is particularly useful for:
Long-term reversible contraception.
Heavy menstrual bleeding, especially with a suitable 52 mg system.
Dysmenorrhoea in selected patients.
Endometrial protection during certain oestrogen replacement regimens, where the specific product and local guidance support this use.
Women who prefer reduced menstrual bleeding.
Women who cannot or prefer not to use oestrogen-containing contraception.
Advantages include:
Very high contraceptive effectiveness.
No daily action required.
Reduced menstrual blood loss in many users.
Possible improvement in dysmenorrhoea.
Fertility generally returns rapidly after removal.
General compatibility with breastfeeding.
Low systemic exposure compared with many systemic hormonal methods, although systemic effects can still occur.
It does not protect against sexually transmitted infections.

content_groups.group_title: A. Irregular bleeding during the first few months

blocks.text: Spotting, irregular bleeding and mild cramping are common after insertion. These usually improve with time.
With continued use, menstruation often becomes lighter, and some women develop amenorrhoea.
Explain this before insertion so the patient understands that early irregular bleeding does not necessarily indicate device failure.
Headache.
Acne or changes in skin condition.
Breast tenderness.
Mood changes in some users.
Pelvic discomfort.
Ovarian cysts, which are often transient.
Not every symptom is necessarily caused by the device, and persistent or severe symptoms require assessment.
Expulsion.
Uterine perforation during insertion.
Pelvic infection, particularly around insertion if an untreated cervical infection is present.
Pregnancy, including ectopic pregnancy if contraceptive failure occurs.
Difficult removal or non-visible threads.
The LNG-IUS does not usually cause permanent infertility. Fertility generally returns rapidly after removal.

subsections.subsection_title: When does the LNG-IUS become effective?

blocks.text: This depends on the timing of insertion, the product and the patient's recent contraceptive history.

For many LNG-IUS products, insertion within the first seven days after menstrual bleeding begins provides immediate contraceptive protection. If inserted later, backup contraception is generally recommended for seven days unless the clinical circumstances or applicable guidance indicate otherwise.
The rules may differ when switching from another method, inserting postpartum or using a particular product for a non-contraceptive indication.
Before insertion, assess whether pregnancy can reasonably be excluded. A negative pregnancy test alone may not rule out conception from very recent intercourse.
This is one of the most important clinical applications of the LNG-IUS.

A suitable 52 mg LNG-IUS can substantially reduce menstrual blood loss and may be an effective treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding when the uterine cavity is suitable and contraindications are absent.

Treat infection according to current guidelines. An IUS does not automatically have to be removed in every case of PID; management depends on clinical response, patient preference and the applicable protocol.

content_groups.group_title: D. Pregnancy with an LNG-IUS in situ

blocks.text: Confirm pregnancy.
Assess urgently for ectopic pregnancy if pain, bleeding or instability is present.
Use transvaginal ultrasound to establish pregnancy location.
Discuss the patient's pregnancy intentions.
If she wishes to continue the pregnancy, arrange specialist assessment and consider early removal when the threads are visible or removal can be performed safely.
Do not attempt blind removal if the threads are not accessible.
Leaving an IUS in place during pregnancy increases the risk of miscarriage, infection and preterm birth.

subsections.subsection_title: Common examiner questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is the difference between a copper IUCD and an LNG-IUS?

The copper IUCD is hormone-free and impairs sperm function. The LNG-IUS releases levonorgestrel, thickens cervical mucus and suppresses the endometrium. The LNG-IUS generally reduces menstrual bleeding, whereas a copper IUCD may increase it.
Q2. Which LNG-IUS is particularly useful for heavy menstrual bleeding?
A suitable 52 mg levonorgestrel-releasing IUS is commonly used, provided the patient is eligible and the uterine cavity is suitable.
Q3. Does the LNG-IUS suppress ovulation?
It may suppress ovulation in some users, but ovulation often continues. Its main contraceptive actions are thickening cervical mucus and local endometrial effects.
Q4. What should you tell a patient about bleeding after insertion?
Irregular bleeding and spotting are common during the first few months. Bleeding generally becomes lighter over time, and some users develop amenorrhoea.
Q5. Can an LNG-IUS be used in a woman who has never given birth?
Yes. Nulliparity alone is not a contraindication.
Q6. Does the LNG-IUS cause infertility?
No. Fertility generally returns rapidly after removal.
Q7. What are the main contraindications?

Important examples include current breast cancer, pregnancy, active pelvic infection at insertion, unexplained bleeding requiring investigation and uterine cavity distortion that prevents correct placement.
Q8. What would you do if a patient has missing threads and pelvic pain?
Assess urgently for pregnancy, ectopic pregnancy, infection, expulsion and perforation. Perform a speculum examination, pregnancy testing and appropriate imaging. Do not attempt blind retrieval.

H — Heavy menstrual bleeding.
O — Obstetric and reproductive history.
R — Relevant medical history.
M — Medications and previous treatments.
O — Other symptoms.
N — Needs and preferences.
E — Eligibility and expectations.
Remember LIGHTER for counselling about the LNG-IUS:
L — Long-acting contraception.
I — Irregular bleeding initially.
G — Generally lighter periods later.
H — Hormonal method, unlike the copper IUCD.
T — Threads and warning symptoms.
E — Evaluate pregnancy and infection risks.
